messages.author: b1a308a5b9312fbc
messages.subject: cenpoisson requirements
parts:
Hi all,

I am modelling a poisson model in INLA, that has no zero values. I want to fit a censored poisson model with interval c(0,max(Y)). I am confused about the documentation pdf where an additional "E" is required as well. What is the meaning of this parameter?

For now I have this:

inla_sp = inla(f,
                  family = "cenpoisson",
                  control.family = list(cenpoisson.I = c(0, max(strandline70$abundance))),
                  data = inla.stack.data(StackFit),
                  control.compute = list(waic=T),
                  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(StackFit))

I also noticed that my spatial fit and autocorrelation change drastically because of this censoring, is this possible?

Kind regards,
Charlotte

messages.author: 936ef8c6d12fc338
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] cenpoisson requirements
parts:
Dear Charlotte,

Why don't you observe zero's? Because you can't observe them? Or because they are not possible? In the latter case a zero-truncated Poisson seems more relevant to me.

inla(
  f,
  family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0",
  control.family = list(
    list(hyper = list(theta = list(initial = -11, fixed = TRUE)))
   )
)

Best regards,

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: cenpoisson requirements
parts:
Hi,

from reading inla.doc("cenpoisson"), I think there's an error in the
documentation, as it says that it deals with values being censored
inside the interval [L, H], but the cenpoisson2 documentation that is
the same except that it allows individual [L, H] values for each
observation seems to make it clear that it is values _outside_ the
interval that is censored.
However, both example codes actually do censor values inside the
intervals (replacing them with L), so there's a clear confusion there;
I'll check with Haavard.

However, what model you need depends on if you have censored
observations (values _outside_ [1,Inf] being censored, setting zeros
to 1), or rather _truncated_ observations, where you've observed Y
from a truncated Poisson distribution, Pr(Y=y | y>0)? In that case
you can use zeroinflatedpoisson1 with a fixed small probability for
zero.

In either case, E is a known scaling constant, so that the Poisson
expectation is defined as E * exp(eta), where eta is the linear
predictor.
E is usually read as "exposure", and used to scale the model with
respect to some known quantity (e.g. population in many cases).

Finn

The cenpoisson/cenpoisson2 documentation is unclear; based on the
initial text and the code examples, it deals with data that cannot
take values inside the given interval and have been replaced by the
lower interval range, L, but the more detailed text for cenpoisson2
seems to say that it deals with ordinary censoring. (In either case I
don't think that's the model Charlotte needs.)

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] cenpoisson requirements
parts:
In this case I think a truncated Poisson is more appropriate (with zeroinflatedpoisson0, like Thierry showed) than an LGCP, unless you do a joint "marked point process model" approach.

Adding zeros on a grid probabilty wouldn't be very helpful, as it would just give you a more expensive way to approximate a marked point process model, and might conflate "did not go there to look for things" with "did not find anything where I looked".

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] cenpoisson requirements
parts:
To clarify around cenpoisson: rereading the cenpoisson2 documentation clarifies how it can be used for both interval- left- and-right censoring.
But in either case, your date is more of the "truncated Poisson" type.

Finn

On Tue, 26 Sept 2023 at 13:23, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
In this case I think a truncated Poisson is more appropriate (with zeroinflatedpoisson0, like Thierry showed) than an LGCP, unless you do a joint "marked point process model" approach.

Adding zeros on a grid probabilty wouldn't be very helpful, as it would just give you a more expensive way to approximate a marked point process model, and might conflate "did not go there to look for things" with "did not find anything where I looked".

Finn

On Tue, 26 Sept 2023 at 12:56, 'Thierry Onkelinx' via R-inla discussion group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
Dear Charlotte,

I presume you want to model the density of plants along the transect. A log Gaussian Cox process model is probably more appropriate. You can fit that with the inlabru package which is an add-on to INLA.
Have a look at the articles on point process examples at https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru

Best regards,

Op di 26 sep 2023 om 13:38 schreef Charlotte Taelman <charlotte...@gmail.com>:
Dear all,

Thank you for your replies.

1) I thought in de documentation the interval could be used to exclude the modelling of the zeros?

E = sample(1:10, N70, replace = T)
inla_sp = inla(f,
                  family = "cenpoisson",
                  control.family = list(cenpoisson.I = c(1, max(strandline70$abundance))),
                  data = inla.stack.data(StackFit),
                  control.compute = list(waic=T),
                  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(StackFit), E = E)

I have been tweaking the E parameter to increase model fit, is this accepted? Howver I still do not get what this parameter means (and does).

2) My data has no zeros as I collected data on plant abundance in the field, where each observation is a geolocated point (X,Y) with an abundance of a plant species on the Belgian coast. Only presences of plants were collected. 
I have tried your code and it works very well! I wonder if it would better to generate zeros (using a grid) and to then have a zero-inflated model?

Kind regards,
Charlotte







Op dinsdag 26 september 2023 om 11:22:08 UTC+2 schreef Thierry Onkelinx:
Dear Charlotte,

Why don't you observe zero's? Because you can't observe them? Or because they are not possible? In the latter case a zero-truncated Poisson seems more relevant to me.

inla(
  f,
  family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0",
  control.family = list(
    list(hyper = list(theta = list(initial = -11, fixed = TRUE)))
   )
)

Best regards,

kind regards,
Charlotte Taelman

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] cenpoisson requirements
parts:
oops, the 'cenpoisson' is cencored in the way that observations in the
interval [L,H] is reported as L, say. this sometimes is done for privacy
reasons, where L=0 and H=5, say.

this is very very different from a case where 0's are not observed. so
there is no 'choice' here, the data collection process dictates what to
use.
